content.title: What is the String Class?
content.description: The String class represents a sequence of characters in Java. Strings are immutable, meaning once a String object is created, its value cannot be changed.

content.content: The String class is one of the most commonly used classes in Java. It is used to store and manipulate textual data. Since strings are immutable, every modification creates a new String object instead of changing the existing one.

content.title: Why Learn Strings?
content.content: Strings are used in almost every Java application for handling names, messages, files, user input, URLs, JSON data, and much more.
Creating Strings
Strings can be created using string literals or by using the new keyword. String literals are stored in the String Pool, while objects created using new are stored in heap memory.

content.title: Creating Strings
content.code:
String s1 = "Java";
String s2 = new String("Programming");

content.title: String Pool
content.description: Java stores string literals in a special memory area called the String Pool to save memory by reusing identical string values.

content.content: String Immutability
Strings are immutable. Whenever a string is modified using methods like concat() or replace(), a new String object is created instead of changing the original object.

content.content: Common String Methods
The String class provides many useful methods for searching, comparing, modifying, and extracting text.
String Comparison
Strings should generally be compared using the equals() method. The == operator compares object references instead of actual string contents.

left_points: May return false for equal text

content.content: String Pool
The String Pool is a special memory area where Java stores string literals. If the same literal already exists, Java reuses the existing object instead of creating another one.

content.title: String Pool Example
Memory Optimization
content.content: The String Pool reduces memory usage by allowing multiple variables to reference the same String object.
StringBuilder and StringBuffer
Since String objects are immutable, Java provides StringBuilder and StringBuffer for efficient modification of character sequences.

content.content: Real-Life Analogy

content.title: Printed Book
content.content: A printed book cannot be modified directly. To change its content, a new edition must be printed. Similarly, modifying a String creates a new object instead of changing the existing one.

content.title: Interview Importance
content.content: Java interviews frequently include questions about String immutability, String Pool, equals() vs ==, StringBuilder vs StringBuffer, and commonly used String methods.
Common Mistakes

items.question: Should == be used for String comparison?
items.answer: No. Use equals() to compare String contents.

items.question: Is concat() modifying the original String?
items.answer: No. It returns a new String object.

content.title: Remember This
content.description: Strings are immutable objects stored efficiently using the String Pool. Use equals() for comparison and StringBuilder for frequent modifications.

content.title: Quick Revision
points: String literals are stored in the String Pool.
Use equals() instead of == for comparing strings.
Common methods include length(), substring(), replace(), and contains().
Use StringBuilder when frequent modifications are required.

content.question: Why are String objects considered immutable?
options: Their value cannot be changed after creation.
They are stored only in RAM.
content.answer: Their value cannot be changed after creation.
